about.title: Lemoore Product Liability Claims
about.longDescription: Defective products show up everywhere in Lemoore life — a faulty piece of farm equipment near the fields off W Hanford Armona Road, a malfunctioning appliance in a home near N Lemoore Avenue, or unsafe auto parts involved in a collision on Rt 41. California generally applies strict liability to these cases, meaning an injured person often doesn't have to prove the manufacturer was negligent, only that the product had a defect and that defect caused harm. Design flaws, manufacturing errors, and inadequate warnings can all support a claim, and liability can extend beyond the manufacturer to distributors and retailers who put the product into the market. If a defective product hurt you or someone in your family here in Kings County, keeping the item itself and any packaging or receipts matters a great deal. LawProactive doesn't practice law — we simply connect you, free of charge, with an independent attorney who can review what happened and explain your options under California law.

items.question: I was hurt by a defective product near W Bush Street — what should I do first?
items.answer: Try to preserve the product exactly as it was when it caused the injury, including any packaging, instructions, or remaining pieces. Photograph the item and the scene if possible, and seek medical attention promptly. Then reach out to LawProactive so we can connect you with an independent attorney who can advise on next steps.

items.question: Do I have to prove the manufacturer was negligent?
items.answer: Not necessarily. California product liability claims often rely on strict liability, meaning you generally need to show the product was defective and that the defect caused your injury, rather than proving the company was careless. An attorney can evaluate which theory best fits your situation.

items.question: Can I still file a claim if the product was bought secondhand or from a local Lemoore retailer?
items.answer: Possibly — liability can extend to retailers and distributors, not just the original manufacturer, depending on how the product moved through the supply chain. Details like where and how the product was purchased can matter, so it's worth discussing your specific situation with an attorney.
